The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T03:56:01Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T03:56:26Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-11T03:50:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) to 2026-11-11T03:57:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 7 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 42 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T03:59:04Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.1% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 0.7% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 2.0% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none - no more of the traffic failed while it was broken than before it began.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 214.63333333333333 ms {series_before} before it began, 2020 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 2230 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault is in `average_spend_per_item` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. For each purchase at position `index`, the loop re-sums `account.purchases[:index + 1]`. Only the last pass's value is kept, so for n purchases the function does n(n+1)/2 price additions and n slice copies to get what one sum gives. Work grows with the square of the history length, which fits the latency step with flat error rate, CPU-per-request shape and volume.
      
      The fix sums `price_cents` across `account.purchases` once and floor-divides by `len(account.purchases)`. This keeps the behaviour the revision meant to add, and that its docstring and existing tests describe: the figure comes from the purchase list, not from the carried `total_cents`, so `test_the_lifetime_average_follows_the_purchases_not_the_carried_total` still holds. For an account with no purchases, the sum is 0 {F1.1} and `0 // 0` still raises ZeroDivisionError. `render_spend_summary` passes that through to its caller as before, so `test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller` is unchanged. The signature and return type are the same, so callers are unaffected.
      
      New test: tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py builds an account of 200 {F1.2} purchase records that count how many times `price_cents` is read. It asserts the count is exactly 200 {F1.3} and that the average is correct. The prefix-re-summing loop would read the price 20,100 {F1.4} times, so the test is written to fail against the current code and pass with one read per purchase.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

      from __future__ import annotations
      
      from io_shop.accounts import Account
      from io_shop.typical_spend import typical_spend_per_item
      
      """What a shopper has spent, and what that averages to.
      
      Three figures about one history. The lifetime average has been on the account
      page for years; the monthly one narrows it to the current month; the typical
      purchase abandons the average altogether for the middle of the history. The
      last two are the ones still behind a rollout, and which of them a request gets
      is decided before it reaches here.
      """
      
      
      def average_spend_per_item(account: Account) -> int:
          """Average spend per item across everything this account has ever bought.
      
          Live for years. Its divisor is empty only for an account that has never
          bought anything at all, which no real shopper is.
      
          Derives the total from the purchases rather than reading the one the account
          carries, taking each purchase in and recomputing what has been spent by
          then, so that the figure agrees with the list the shopper is looking at even
          where the totals the query returned have drifted from it.
          """
          spent_by_then = 0 {S1.1}
      
          for index, _ in enumerate(account.purchases):
              spent_by_then = sum(
                  earlier.price_cents for earlier in account.purchases[:index + 1 {S1.2}]
              )
      
          return spent_by_then // len(account.purchases)
      
      
      def average_spend_per_item_this_month(account: Account) -> int:
          """Average spend per item this month.
      
          Narrows the lifetime figure to the current month, so the account page can
          show what a shopper is spending now rather than what they averaged over
          three years.
          """
          bought_this_month = [
              purchase for purchase in account.purchases if purchase.in_current_month
          ]
          return account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)
      
      
      def render_spend_summary(account: Account,
                               use_monthly_summary: bool,
                               use_typical_spend: bool = False) -> int:
          """The figure Io's account page shows, through whichever version the rollout
          selects.
      
          Raises whatever the selected version raises. Catching belongs at the request
          boundary - see `io_shop.account_page` - where there is a response to turn a
          failure into and a log to record it in. A page that swallowed its own errors
          would render a wrong number instead of an error, which is a worse incident
          than the one it hid.
      
          Two rollouts, so two flags to be told about, and the newer one wins where a
          request is inside both. That is the ordinary arrangement: each is a slice of
          traffic, the slices overlap, and the page has to render one figure.
          """
          if use_typical_spend:
              return typical_spend_per_item(account)
      
          if use_monthly_summary:
              return average_spend_per_item_this_month(account)
      
          return average_spend_per_item(account)
      
  - [S2] tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py at 5e07d73
      from __future__ import annotations
      
      import pytest
      from io_shop.accounts import Account, Purchase
      from io_shop.spend_summary import (
          average_spend_per_item,
          average_spend_per_item_this_month,
          render_spend_summary,
      )
      
      """Io's account-page arithmetic - the lifetime figure and the monthly one.
      
      The monthly figure is newer and ships behind a rollout flag, so the cases below
      cover the shape the page has had for years plus the one the flag adds.
      """
      
      
      def an_account_with_no_purchases_this_month(*prices: int) -> Account:
          """The ordinary case: a shopper who has bought before, but not this month."""
          return Account(
              shopper_id="shopper-idle-this-month",
              purchases=tuple(
                  Purchase(price_cents=price, in_current_month=False) for price in prices
              ),
              total_cents=sum(prices),
              total_this_month_cents=0,
          )
      
      
      def test_the_lifetime_average_spreads_the_total_over_every_purchase() -> None:
          account = an_account_with_no_purchases_this_month(1000, 2000 {S2.1}, 3000 {S2.2})
      
          assert average_spend_per_item(account) == 2000 {S2.3}
      
      
      def test_the_lifetime_average_follows_the_purchases_not_the_carried_total() -> None:
          # The figure is derived from the list the shopper is looking at, so a total
          # that has drifted from its own purchases does not reach the page.
          an_account_whose_total_drifted = Account(
              shopper_id="shopper-with-a-stale-total",
              purchases=(
                  Purchase(price_cents=1000, in_current_month=False),
                  Purchase(price_cents=3000, in_current_month=False),
              ),
              total_cents=99_999,
              total_this_month_cents=0,
          )
      
          assert average_spend_per_item(an_account_whose_total_drifted) == 2000 {S2.4}
      
      
      def test_the_monthly_average_is_correct_for_a_shopper_who_did_buy() -> None:
          # The ordinary case for the monthly figure: a shopper who has bought
          # something this month, averaged over what they bought this month.
          an_active_shopper = Account(
              shopper_id="shopper-who-bought-this-month",
              purchases=(
                  Purchase(price_cents=4000, in_current_month=True),
                  Purchase(price_cents=2000, in_current_month=True),
                  Purchase(price_cents=9000, in_current_month=False),
              ),
              total_cents=15000,
              total_this_month_cents=6000,
          )
      
          assert average_spend_per_item_this_month(an_active_shopper) == 3000 {S2.5}
      
      
      def test_the_page_takes_the_stable_summary_when_the_rollout_is_off() -> None:
          account = an_account_with_no_purchases_this_month(1000, 3000 {S2.6})
      
          assert render_spend_summary(account, use_monthly_summary=False) == 2000 {S2.7}
      
      
      def test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller() -> None:
          # Swallowing it here would render a wrong number instead of an error, and
          # there would be no error rate for anyone to alert on.
          a_shopper_who_never_bought_anything = Account(
              shopper_id="shopper-with-no-history", purchases=(), total_cents=0,
              total_this_month_cents=0
          )
      
          with pytest.raises(ZeroDivisionError):
              render_spend_summary(
                  a_shopper_who_never_bought_anything, use_monthly_summary=False
              )

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: average_spend_per_item was rewritten so that, for every purchase in an account's history, it re-sums the prices of all purchases up to that point and keeps only the last pass. The work per call therefore grows with the square of the number of purchases, where before it was a single division of the account's carried total. render_spend_summary takes this path for the account page's figure whenever neither rollout flag is set.
cause_in_plain_words: A software update changed how the shop works out a shopper's average spend per item: it now adds up the shopper's past purchases again for each purchase in turn, so the more a shopper had bought, the more work each page took.
still_at_risk: Revision 5e07d73 still holds the slow calculation, and deploying it or anything built on it again would slow the shop's responses in the same way.
symptom: Shoppers' requests to the shop were answered far more slowly than usual
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' requests to io-shop were answered far more slowly than usual, while no larger share of them failed than before. (cites AL1)
causal_chain 2: Deploy P2 by kuki at {P2.1} put revision 5e07d73 on io-shop, in the minute the onset was placed in. As of {T11.1}, all replicas ran that revision, so the slowdown was not a split between versions. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; T6, under "What Argus did, in order"; T11, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 2 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy P1 of revision 70dbcfd: the metrics read show the service healthy with it in place until the onset, and rolling back to it returned the service to normal, which was confirmed. (cites T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; T6, under "What Argus did, in order"; T23, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3: The revision rewrote average_spend_per_item, the function render_spend_summary calls for the account page's lifetime figure when neither rollout flag is set. It replaced dividing the account's carried total by its number of purchases with a loop that, for each purchase, re-sums the prices of every purchase up to that one. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
causal_chain 4: Each call now did work that grows with the square of the shopper's purchase count instead of a single division, so pages that showed the figure took far longer to compute. (cites D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
contributing_factors 1: No check of how long the account-page calculations take on a long purchase history was seen before the change went out. The tests at the revision check only correct values, on accounts with a handful of purchases.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: A check timing average_spend_per_item on a long history would have failed on the prefix-re-summing loop, and the revision would have been stopped before it reached production.
contributing_factors 2: No staged or canary rollout was seen: the revision reached every replica, with nothing seen comparing latency on new replicas against the earlier revision before the rollout completed.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: The slowdown would have reached only part of the traffic and could have halted the rollout before every shopper's requests were slowed.
action_items 1: Add a check to io-shop's pipeline that times the account-page summary functions on accounts with long purchase histories and fails any change whose cost grows beyond a set bound.
action_items 2: Roll io-shop deployments out to a canary replica first, and hold the rollout while that replica's p95 latency is compared with replicas still on the earlier revision.
action_items 3: Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
went_wrong 1: Nobody was paged: the alert fired but was not linked to an on-call incident, so no person was called in to the response.
